claims.claim: HOIP is destabilized in cells lacking SHARPIN or HOIL-1L.
claims.source: Given that HOIP is destabilized in cells lacking SHARPIN or HOIL-1L (Gerlach et al., 2011; Ikeda et al., 2011; Tokunaga et al., 2011; Fujita et al., 2018; Peltzer et al., 2018)
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Co-expression of HOIP, HOIL-1L, and SHARPIN in insect cells enabled isolation of recombinant LUBAC with no major contaminants.
claims.source: Using this co-expression strategy, we were able to isolate three proteins of the expected molecular weights with no major contaminants as determined by SDS-PAGE followed by Coomassie staining (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: The identities of the co-purified proteins were verified as the three LUBAC components by immunoblotting.
claims.source: Furthermore, we verified the identities of these proteins as the three LUBAC components by immunoblotting indicating the successful isolation of recombinant LUBAC (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: Gel filtration chromatography of purified LUBAC showed two main peaks eluting earlier than the 158 kDa molecular weight standard.
claims.source: The elution profile of the complex contained two peaks eluting at 0.942 ml (peak I) and 0.972 ml (peak II) as well as one minor peak eluting at 1.158 ml (peak III). All of these peaks eluted earlier than the 158 kDa molecular weight standard, which eluted at 1.246 ml (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by gel filtration data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Peaks I and II from gel filtration contained all LUBAC components.
claims.source: However, while peaks I and II contained all LUBAC components, peak III contained predominantly HOIL-1L and SHARPIN (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, lower panel) indicating the presence of partially assembled complexes.
claims.evidence: This is supported by gel filtration data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Peak III from gel filtration contained predominantly HOIL-1L and SHARPIN.
claims.source: However, while peaks I and II contained all LUBAC components, peak III contained predominantly HOIL-1L and SHARPIN (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, lower panel) indicating the presence of partially assembled complexes.
claims.evidence: This is supported by gel filtration data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Tandem gel filtration of peak II showed that the complex is not prone to dissociation after purification.
claims.source: The elution profile from this second tandem run contained almost exclusively peaks I and II, which correspond to assembled LUBAC (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, lower panel). Conversely, peak III was almost entirely absent from the elution profile indicating that the complex is not prone to dissociation after purification.
claims.evidence: This is supported by tandem gel filtration data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Negative staining electron microscopy showed a monodisperse distribution of LUBAC particles.
claims.source: Micrographs show a monodisperse distribution of particles of similar size, which could be sorted into 2D class averages showing a distinct elongated dumbbell structure thus verifying the homogeneity of the sample (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The first low-resolution 3D reconstruction of LUBAC was generated from negative stain electron microscopy.
claims.source: Furthermore, we were able to generate the first low-resolution 3D reconstruction of LUBAC from these particles (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the 3D reconstruction shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The 3D model of LUBAC displays an elongated asymmetric crescent structure with the majority of mass concentrated at one end.
claims.source: In accordance with the class averages, the model displays an elongated asymmetric crescent structure with the majority of the mass concentrated at one end.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the 3D reconstruction shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Mass photometry measurements showed that the majority of LUBAC species had average masses of 231 kDa and 454 kDa.
claims.source: MP measurements showed that the majority of species present in the samples had average masses of 231 kDa (peak II) and 454 kDa (peak III) (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by mass photometry data shown in Figure 2D and Supplementary file 1.

claims.claim: The populations of peaks II and III from mass photometry nearly correspond with monomers (222 kDa) and dimers (444 kDa) of LUBAC with a 1:1:1 stoichiometry.
claims.source: With respect to the expected mass of the ternary LUBAC, the populations of peaks II and III nearly correspond with monomers (222 kDa) and dimers (444 kDa) of LUBAC with a 1:1:1 stoichiometry between HOIP, HOIL-1L, and SHARPIN.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the mass photometry data.

claims.claim: HOIL-1L and SHARPIN interact with HOIP through their respective UBL domains, which bind cooperatively to the HOIP UBA domain.
claims.source: Structural work of protein fragments has shown that HOIL-1L and SHARPIN interact with HOIP through their respective ubiquitin-like (UBL) domains, which bind cooperatively to the HOIP UBA domain (Fujita et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2017; Yagi et al., 2012; Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: The SHARPIN UBL domain interacts with the NZF2 domain of HOIP.
claims.source: By using truncation mutants, it has also been shown that the SHARPIN UBL domain interacts with the Npl zinc finger 2 (NZF2) domain of HOIP (Ikeda et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: SHARPIN and HOIL-1L interact with each other through their respective LTMs.
claims.source: More recently, structural work has revealed that SHARPIN and HOIL-1L interact with each other through their respective LUBAC-tethering motifs (LTMs) (Fujita et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: Cross-linking mass spectrometry revealed an extensive network of intra-protein and inter-protein cross-links in LUBAC.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 3B–E, we observed an extensive network of intra-protein and inter-protein cross-links, providing a detailed picture of LUBAC assembly (Figure 3B–E, Supplementary files 2 and 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by cross-linking mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3 and supplementary files.

claims.claim: HOIL-1L K174, SHARPIN K318, and HOIP K454/458 are highly cross-linking residues that formed cross-links indiscriminately to all subunits.
claims.source: We detected some highly cross-linking residues that formed cross-links indiscriminately to all subunits of all proteins. These were HOIL-1L K174, SHARPIN K318, and HOIP K454/458.
claims.evidence: This is supported by cross-linking mass spectrometry data.

claims.claim: The highly cross-linking residues are likely located on flexible regions.
claims.source: The high degree of cross-linking formed by these residues suggests that they are located on flexible regions.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the cross-linking pattern.

claims.claim: Cross-links were observed between the HOIL-1L RING1 and HOIP RING1/LDD domains.
claims.source: Interestingly, we observed cross-links between the HOIL-1L RING1 and HOIP RING1/LDD domains, as well as between the HOIL-1L RING2 and the HOIP RING1/IBR/RING2/LDD domains, which suggest that the two enzymes have spatially connected catalytic activities.
claims.evidence: This is supported by cross-linking mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Cross-links were observed between the HOIL-1L RING2 and the HOIP RING1/IBR/RING2/LDD domains.
claims.source: Interestingly, we observed cross-links between the HOIL-1L RING1 and HOIP RING1/LDD domains, as well as between the HOIL-1L RING2 and the HOIP RING1/IBR/RING2/LDD domains, which suggest that the two enzymes have spatially connected catalytic activities.
claims.evidence: This is supported by cross-linking mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The two enzymes HOIP and HOIL-1L have spatially connected catalytic activities.
claims.source: Interestingly, we observed cross-links between the HOIL-1L RING1 and HOIP RING1/LDD domains, as well as between the HOIL-1L RING2 and the HOIP RING1/IBR/RING2/LDD domains, which suggest that the two enzymes have spatially connected catalytic activities.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the cross-linking data.

claims.claim: HOIL-1L intra-protein cross-links were formed between its NZF domain and its RING1/IBR/RING2 domains.
claims.source: Additionally, HOIL-1L intra-protein cross-links were formed between its NZF domain and its RING1/IBR/RING2 domains, which could implicate the HOIL-1L NZF domain of unknown function in the catalytic action of HOIL-1L.
claims.evidence: This is supported by cross-linking mass spectrometry data.

claims.claim: The catalytic RBR domains of HOIP and HOIL-1L are close to each other.
claims.source: In conclusion, the catalytic RBR domains of HOIP and HOIL1L seem to be close to each other, as well as the NZF and RBR regions of HOIL-1L.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the cross-linking data.

claims.claim: LUBAC may have a single catalytic centre containing the RBR domains of HOIP and HOIL-1L.
claims.source: These data suggest that LUBAC may have a single catalytic centre containing the RBR domains of HOIP and HOIL-1L.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the cross-linking data.

claims.claim: Recombinant LUBAC generated linear ubiquitin chains in an ATP-dependent manner.
claims.source: As expected, LUBAC generated linear ubiquitin chains in an ATP-dependent manner (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vitro ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Additional signals were observed from co-purified LUBAC that were absent from reactions containing individually purified and mixed LUBAC components.
claims.source: We also observed additional signals derived from co-purified LUBAC, which were absent from reactions containing the three individually purified and mixed LUBAC components (Figure 4B: red arrows).
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vitro ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Mixing HOIP, HOIL-1L, and SHARPIN does not suffice to assemble LUBAC.
claims.source: The absence of these populations indicates that mixing HOIP, HOIL-1L, and SHARPIN does not suffice to assemble LUBAC.
claims.evidence: This is supported by mass photometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Heterotypic ubiquitin chain assembly was observed with all tested ubiquitin KR mutants (K6R, K11R, K27R, K29R, K33R, K48R, and K63R).
claims.source: Heterotypic ubiquitin chain assembly was observed with all the tested mutants, K6R, K11R, K27R, K29R, K33R, K48R, and K63R.
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vitro ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: The K0 ubiquitin mutant could be used by LUBAC to generate heterotypic ubiquitin chains.
claims.source: Despite reduced reaction efficiency, the K0 mutant could also be used by LUBAC to generate the heterotypic ubiquitin chains.
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vitro ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: The additional signals from ubiquitin chains assembled by LUBAC disappeared by treatment with Cezanne, a DUB specific for the Lys11 linkage.
claims.source: Interestingly, the additional signals from ubiquitin chains assembled by LUBAC disappeared by treatment with Cezanne, a DUB specific for the Lys11 linkage (Bremm et al., 2010); or vOTU, a DUB targeting Lys linkages (Akutsu et al., 2011; Figure 4E; upper red arrow).
claims.evidence: This is supported by UbiCRest data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: The additional signals from ubiquitin chains assembled by LUBAC disappeared by treatment with vOTU, a DUB targeting Lys linkages.
claims.source: Interestingly, the additional signals from ubiquitin chains assembled by LUBAC disappeared by treatment with Cezanne, a DUB specific for the Lys11 linkage (Bremm et al., 2010); or vOTU, a DUB targeting Lys linkages (Akutsu et al., 2011; Figure 4E; upper red arrow).
claims.evidence: This is supported by UbiCRest data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: The linear linkage-specific DUB OTULIN hydrolysed all linear ubiquitin bonds but left non-linear di- and tri-ubiquitin residues.
claims.source: The linear linkage-specific DUB OTULIN (Fiil et al., 2013) hydrolysed all linear ubiquitin bonds (Figure 4E: upper panel), corresponding to most of the ubiquitin signal, but left non-linear di- and tri-ubiquitin residues (Figure 4E: lower panel).
claims.evidence: This is supported by UbiCRest data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: Recombinant LUBAC assembles heterotypic ubiquitin chains containing predominantly linear linkage with non-Lys-linked branches.
claims.source: These data collectively indicate that recombinant LUBAC assembles heterotypic ubiquitin chains containing predominantly linear linkage with non-Lys-linked branches.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple experimental results.

claims.claim: Treatment with hydroxylamine resulted in the disappearance of the upper band of the linear tetra-ubiquitin chain assembled by LUBAC.
claims.source: Treatment with hydroxylamine resulted in the disappearance of the upper band of the linear tetra-ubiquitin chain (Figure 5A: red arrow).
claims.evidence: This is supported by hydroxylamine treatment data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: The chain branching in LUBAC-assembled ubiquitin chains is achieved by formation of an oxyester bond between ubiquitin moieties.
claims.source: This indicates that the chain branching is achieved by formation of an oxyester bond between ubiquitin moieties similar to the observation in the previous study (Kelsall et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on hydroxylamine sensitivity and comparison to previous literature.

claims.claim: LUBAC inefficiently assembled di- and tri-ubiquitin chains with His-ubiquitin, which are sensitive to hydroxylamine treatment.
claims.source: LUBAC inefficiently assembled di- and tri-ubiquitin chains with His-ubiquitin, which are sensitive to hydroxylamine treatment (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vitro ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: When the N-terminus of ubiquitin is not available, LUBAC can still assemble oxyester-linked poly-ubiquitin even in the absence of linear ubiquitin chains.
claims.source: These results demonstrate that when the N-terminus of ubiquitin is not available, LUBAC can still assemble oxyester-linked poly-ubiquitin even in the absence of linear ubiquitin chains.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the His-ubiquitin experiment.

claims.claim: Treatment with OTULIN and hydroxylamine resulted in complete degradation of the poly-ubiquitin signals from LUBAC-assembled chains.
claims.source: Restriction with OTULIN degraded the majority of the signal from ubiquitin chains leaving short di- and tri-ubiquitin polymers. Subsequent treatment with hydroxylamine resulted in complete degradation of the poly-ubiquitin signals.
claims.evidence: This is supported by combined OTULIN and hydroxylamine treatment data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: LUBAC assembles exclusively OTULIN-sensitive linear and hydroxylamine-sensitive oxyester linkages between ubiquitin moieties.
claims.source: These results indicate that LUBAC assembles exclusively OTULIN-sensitive linear and hydroxylamine-sensitive oxyester linkages between ubiquitin moieties.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined OTULIN and hydroxylamine treatment.

claims.claim: MS/MS spectra of GG-conjugated dipeptides at residues Thr12 and Thr55 of ubiquitin were detected from LUBAC-assembled ubiquitin chains.
claims.source: MS/MS spectra of GG-conjugated dipeptides at residues Thr12 and Thr55 of ubiquitin were detected from these samples, in which there was complete coverage of the ubiquitin amino acid sequence 1–73 (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Thr12 and Thr55 are positioned at opposite sides of ubiquitin and neither is located in proximity to Met1 or the C-terminal Gly76.
claims.source: Structural analysis shows that these two residues are positioned at opposite sides of ubiquitin and neither of them is located in proximity to Met1 or the C-terminal Gly76 (Figure 5D; PDB:1UBI).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural analysis of ubiquitin shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Individual or concomitant mutation of Thr12 and Thr55 did not result in loss of chain branching.
claims.source: Individual or concomitant mutation of Thr12 and Thr55 (Ub T12V, Ub T55V, or Ub T12/55V, respectively) did not result in loss of chain branching.
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vitro ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: Linear chain branching is not a strictly site-specific event.
claims.source: These results suggest that linear chain branching is not a strictly site-specific event.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the Thr mutant experiments.

claims.claim: TNF stimulation increased formation of linear ubiquitin chains in MEFs.
claims.source: TNF stimulation increased formation of linear ubiquitin chains detected by immunoblotting using an antibody specific for linear ubiquitin chains (Figure 6A: PD top panel lane 7).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GST pull-down data from TNF-stimulated MEFs shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Linear ubiquitin chains formed in TNF-stimulated MEFs proved sensitive to hydroxylamine treatment.
claims.source: These chains proved sensitive to hydroxylamine treatment (Figure 6A: PD top panel lane 8).
claims.evidence: This is supported by hydroxylamine treatment data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Ubiquitin chains containing both linear linkages and hydroxylamine-sensitive ester bonds are produced in cells in response to TNF stimulation.
claims.source: Together these results suggest that ubiquitin chains containing both linear linkages and hydroxylamine-sensitive ester bonds are produced in cells in response to TNF stimulation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the TNF stimulation and hydroxylamine treatment experiments.

claims.claim: Treatment of ubiquitinated NEMO with hydroxylamine resulted in enrichment of some lower molecular weight bands.
claims.source: Treatment of ubiquitinated NEMO with the compound resulted in enrichment of some lower molecular weight bands corresponding to ubiquitinated NEMO when blotting with a NEMO-specific antibody.
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vitro ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: The majority of the signal from ubiquitinated NEMO was unperturbed by hydroxylamine treatment.
claims.source: However, the majority of the signal from the ubiquitinated NEMO was unperturbed.
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vitro ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: The conjugation of ubiquitin chains to NEMO is principally through hydroxylamine-resistant isopeptide bonds with some hydroxylamine-sensitive chain branching.
claims.source: These results suggest that the conjugation of ubiquitin chains to the substrate is principally through hydroxylamine-resistant isopeptide bonds with some hydroxylamine-sensitive chain branching or substrate ubiquitination also taking place on longer linear chains.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the NEMO ubiquitination and hydroxylamine treatment data.

claims.claim: HOIP assembles linear ubiquitin chains through the action of its RBR domains wherein Cys885 is the catalytic residue.
claims.source: HOIP specifically assembles linear ubiquitin chains through the action of its RBR domains wherein Cys885 is the catalytic residue (Smit et al., 2012; Stieglitz et al., 2013)
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: HOIL-1L catalyses ester bond-directed ubiquitination via its RBR domain where Cys460 is the catalytic site.
claims.source: similarly HOIL-1L catalyses ester bond-directed ubiquitination via its RBR domain where Cys460 is the catalytic site (Kelsall et al., 2019; Smit et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: LUBAC containing HOIL-1L C460A generated chains with linear linkages, yet the double band indicative of heterotypic chain assembly was absent.
claims.source: In line with our hypothesis, LUBAC containing HOIL-1L C460A generated chains with linear linkages, yet the double band indicative of heterotypic chain assembly was absent (Figure 7A; lane 6 upper red arrow).
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vitro ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: HOIL-1L is responsible for the formation of the ester-linked branches.
claims.source: These observations indicate that HOIL-1L is responsible for the formation of the ester-linked branches.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the HOIL-1L C460A mutant data.

claims.claim: HOIP assembled longer linear ubiquitin chains in the absence of HOIL-1L catalytic activity and did so more rapidly.
claims.source: Consistent with previous reports (Smit et al., 2013; Fuseya et al., 2020), HOIP assembled longer linear ubiquitin chains in the absence of HOIL-1L catalytic activity and did so more rapidly (Figure 7A: lanes 2 and 6).
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vitro ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 7A and is consistent with previous reports.

claims.claim: LUBAC containing HOIP C885A was incapable of polymerizing ubiquitin.
claims.source: Conversely, LUBAC containing HOIP C885A was incapable of polymerizing ubiquitin altogether (Figure 7A; lanes 4 and 8) as expected.
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vitro ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: HOIL-1L catalytic activity disturbs linear ubiquitin chain formation but requires HOIP catalytic activity.
claims.source: These results suggest that HOIL-1L catalytic activity disturbs linear ubiquitin chain formation but requires HOIP catalytic activity.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the catalytic mutant experiments.

claims.claim: The ubiquitin chains assembled by LUBAC contained non-linear di- and tri-ubiquitin chains.
claims.source: The restriction analyses showed that the ubiquitin chains assembled by LUBAC contained non-linear di- and tri-ubiquitin chains, whereas chains assembled by HOIL-1L C460A-containing LUBAC generated exclusively OTULIN-sensitive linear ubiquitin chains (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by OTULIN restriction data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Chains assembled by HOIL-1L C460A-containing LUBAC generated exclusively OTULIN-sensitive linear ubiquitin chains.
claims.source: The restriction analyses showed that the ubiquitin chains assembled by LUBAC contained non-linear di- and tri-ubiquitin chains, whereas chains assembled by HOIL-1L C460A-containing LUBAC generated exclusively OTULIN-sensitive linear ubiquitin chains (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by OTULIN restriction data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: The expression levels of the three LUBAC components are similar in Rbck1+/+ and Rbck1C458A/C458A MEFs.
claims.source: The expression levels of the three LUBAC components are similar in MEFs in Rbck1+/+ and Rbck1C458A/C458A MEFs (Figure 7—figure supplement 2D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2D.

claims.claim: TNF stimulation led to an increase in the levels of linear ubiquitin chains in Rbck1C458A/C458A MEFs.
claims.source: Similarly, to WT MEFs, TNF stimulation led to an increase in the levels of linear ubiquitin chains in Rbck1C458A/C458A MEFs (Figure 7C: PD top panel lanes 3 and 7).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GST pull-down data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: Rbck1C458A/C458A MEFs showed a higher basal level of linear ubiquitin chains compared to Rbck1+/+ MEFs.
claims.source: However, the enriched ubiquitin signals detected by immunoblotting revealed a higher basal level of linear ubiquitin chains in Rbck1C458A/C458A MEFs compared to those in Rbck1+/+ MEFs (Figure 7C: PD top panel lanes 1 and 5).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GST pull-down data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: Linear ubiquitin chains in Rbck1C458A/C458A MEFs were not sensitive to degradation by hydroxylamine treatment.
claims.source: Moreover, unlike in Rbck1+/+ MEFs, linear ubiquitin chains in Rbck1C458A/C458A MEFs were not sensitive to degradation by hydroxylamine treatment (Figure 7C: PD bottom panel).
claims.evidence: This is supported by hydroxylamine treatment data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: Ester-linked branching of linear ubiquitin chains formed during TNF signalling in MEFs is dependent on the catalytic activity of HOIL-1L.
claims.source: These results show that ester-linked branching of linear ubiquitin chains formed during TNF signalling in MEFs is dependent on the catalytic activity of HOIL-1L.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the Rbck1C458A/C458A MEF experiments.

claims.claim: Chain branching activity by LUBAC was partially impaired by the HOIL-1L T203A,R210A mutant.
claims.source: In agreement with our hypothesis, chain branching activity by LUBAC was partially impaired by the HOIL-1L T203A,R210A mutant when compared to the WT or HOIL-1L C460A (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vitro ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: LUBAC with HOIL-1L T203A,R210A assembled ubiquitin chains more efficiently than WT LUBAC but less efficiently than HOIL-1L C460.
claims.source: Interestingly, LUBAC with HOIL-1L T203A,R210A assembled ubiquitin chains more efficiently than WT LUBAC but less efficiently than HOIL-1L C460 (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vitro ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: HOIP assembles linear ubiquitin chains, which are subsequently branched by HOIL-1L in a process involving its NZF domain.
claims.source: These data collectively show that HOIP assembles linear ubiquitin chains, which are subsequently branched by HOIL-1L in a process involving its NZF domain and which requires the catalytic activity of HOIP.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple experimental results.

claims.claim: The 3D map obtained from negative stain electron micrographs shows a particle of elongated structure.
claims.source: This discrepancy would also be accounted for by a particle of non-globular structure, which would elute earlier than expected from a gel filtration column (Siegel and Monty, 1966; Erickson, 2009). Accordingly, the 3D map we obtained from negative stain electron micrographs shows a particle of elongated structure.
claims.evidence: This is based on the 3D reconstruction data and comparison to gel filtration behavior.

claims.claim: A catalytic Cys relay mechanism is proposed in LUBAC where HOIP receives ubiquitin from the E2 and uses it to assemble linear chains or transfers it to HOIL-1L.
claims.source: We propose a catalytic Cys relay mechanism in LUBAC: HOIP receives ubiquitin from the E2 and uses this ubiquitin to assemble linear chains or transfers it to HOIL-1L, which then branches the chains assisted by its NZF domain (Figure 8).
claims.evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental data and illustrated in Figure 8.

claims.claim: MYCBP2 is an example of an E3 ligase with a relay mechanism that conjugates ubiquitin to Thr residues through an ester bond.
claims.source: One recent example of such a mechanism is the E3 ligase MYCBP2, which also conjugates the ubiquitin to Thr residues through an ester bond (Pao et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to literature.

claims.claim: A relay mechanism would require spatial proximity between the catalytic sites of HOIP and HOIL-1L.
claims.source: A relay mechanism would require spatial proximity between the catalytic sites of the two ligases.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference about the requirements for a relay mechanism.

claims.claim: Cross-linking mass spectrometry data show spatial proximity between the catalytic sites of HOIP and HOIL-1L based on cross-linking between their RBR domains.
claims.source: Our XL-MS data show that this is indeed the case based on cross-linking between the RBR domains of HOIP and HOIL-1L.
claims.evidence: This is based on the cross-linking mass spectrometry data.

claims.claim: LUBAC has a single catalytic centre containing the RBR domains of HOIP and HOIL-1L.
claims.source: Collectively, these observations suggest that LUBAC has a single catalytic centre containing the RBR domains of HOIP and HOIL-1L.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the cross-linking data.

claims.claim: HOIP exclusively targets Met1 of a ubiquitin moiety for polymerization.
claims.source: HOIP and HOIL-1L have distinct catalytic behaviour. HOIP exclusively targets Met1 of a ubiquitin moiety for polymerization (Swatek et al., 2019)
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: HOIL-1L has more flexibility with target sites in forming ester bonds.
claims.source: in contrast, HOIL-1L seems to have more flexibility with target sites in forming ester bonds.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing multiple target sites.

claims.claim: Thr12 and Thr55 in ubiquitin were identified as target sites for ester bond formation by mass spectrometry.
claims.source: We identified Thr12 and Thr55 in ubiquitin as target sites by mass spectrometry
claims.evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Individual and concomitant mutation of Thr12 and Thr55 did not abolish heterotypic chain assembly suggesting existence of secondary sites.
claims.source: yet individual and concomitant mutation of these residues did not abolish heterotypic chain assembly suggesting existence of secondary sites.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the Thr mutant experiments shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: A recent study identified Thr12, Ser20, and Thr22, but not Thr55, as target sites by isolated HOIL-1L.
claims.source: A recent study identified Thr12, Ser20, and Thr22, but not Thr55, as target sites by isolated HOIL-1L (Kelsall et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claims.claim: HOIP and SHARPIN may contribute to site selection for HOIL-1L catalytic activity.
claims.source: These differences may depend on HOIL-1L as an isolated protein, or HOIL-1L as a part of LUBAC where HOIP and SHARPIN contribute to site selection.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the differences observed between isolated HOIL-1L and HOIL-1L in LUBAC.

claims.claim: HOIP and SHARPIN contribute to the catalytic action of HOIL-1L based on loss of HOIL-1L auto-ubiquitination signal in cells lacking these proteins.
claims.source: We speculate that HOIP and SHARPIN contribute to the catalytic action of HOIL-1L based on the observed loss of the HOIL-1L auto-ubiquitination signal in cells derived from SHARPIN-deficient mice (Gerlach et al., 2011; Ikeda et al., 2011; Tokunaga et al., 2011) and HOIP knockout mice (Peltzer et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on observations from knockout mice studies.

claims.claim: The oxyester branch points of ubiquitin chains are located distally from the substrate.
claims.source: Our analysis of chain branching on substrate-conjugated ubiquitin chains suggests that the oxyester branch points of the chain are located distally from the substrate.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the NEMO ubiquitination and hydroxylamine treatment data.

claims.claim: Linear ubiquitin chains are not conjugated onto NEMO via oxyester bonds.
claims.source: Treatment of NEMO in vitro ubiquitination reactions resulted in some change of signal, but the overall levels of ubiquitinated substrate were unperturbed, indicating that linear ubiquitin chains are not conjugated onto NEMO via oxyester bonds.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the NEMO ubiquitination and hydroxylamine treatment data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Loss of HOIL-1L catalytic activity impairs but does not prevent conjugation of linear ubiquitin chains to LUBAC substrates IRAK1, IRAK2, and MyD88.
claims.source: This is consistent with a previous report showing that loss of HOIL-1L catalytic activity impairs but does not prevent conjugation of linear ubiquitin chains to the LUBAC substrates IRAK1, IRAK2, and MyD88 (Kelsall et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous report.

claims.claim: HOIL-1L is not responsible for priming substrates with a mono-ubiquitin that is then extended into a linear ubiquitin chain by HOIP.
claims.source: Our results would also suggest that HOIL-1L is not responsible for priming substrates with a mono-ubiquitin that is then extended into an linear ubiquitin chain by HOIP.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results.

claims.claim: Linear ubiquitin chains are heavily branched in cells.
claims.source: Our data suggests that linear ubiquitin chains are heavily branched in cells.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the hydroxylamine treatment data from cells.

claims.claim: Hydroxylamine treatment results in a near complete loss of signal from linear ubiquitin chains in cells.
claims.source: Hydroxylamine treatment results in a near complete loss of signal from linear ubiquitin chains in cells, which suggests that linear chains are heavily branched.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the hydroxylamine treatment data from cells shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Only small populations of linear chains are successfully branched in vitro.
claims.source: In contrast, our in vitro data suggests that only small populations of linear chains are successfully branched.
claims.evidence: This is an observation based on the in vitro ubiquitination assay data.

claims.claim: There may be other factors present in cells that assist HOIL-1L in the process of chain branching.
claims.source: One explanation could be that there are other factors present in cells that assist HOIL-1L in the process of chain branching and which remain hitherto unidentified.
claims.evidence: This is speculation to explain the difference between in vitro and cellular data.

claims.claim: Cezanne can cleave the ester-linked branches in vitro.
claims.source: Our data show that a fragment of Cezanne, a DUB specific for Lys11 linkages (Bremm et al., 2010; Mevissen et al., 2016), can cleave the ester-linked branches in vitro.
claims.evidence: This is supported by UbiCRest data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: Cezanne is a known negative regulator of NF-κB.
claims.source: Cezanne is a known negative regulator of NF-κB (Enesa et al., 2008; Evans et al., 2003; Evans et al., 2001; Luong et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Cezanne may have esterase activity and target LUBAC-assembled chains during its counteraction of NF-κB activation.
claims.source: It is therefore tempting to speculate that it has esterase activity and targets the LUBAC-assembled chains during its counteraction of NF-κB activation.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the observed ester-cleaving activity of Cezanne.

claims.claim: HOIL-1L ligase activity regulates TNF-induced signalling and apoptosis.
claims.source: A recent study using HOIL-1L ΔRBR mice and HOIL-1L knock-in cell of ligase inactive mutant showed that HOIL-1L ligase activity regulates TNF-induced signalling and apoptosis (Fuseya et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claims.claim: HOIL-1L Cys458 mutant as a part of LUBAC increased the linear ubiquitination signal in comparison to the WT control.
claims.source: In line with their observations, we also observed that HOIL-1L Cys458 mutant as a part of LUBAC increased the linear ubiquitination signal in comparison to the WT control.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: RIPK1 in the TNF complex is linearly ubiquitinated at increased levels in HOIL-1L catalytic mutant cells.
claims.source: They also showed that RIPK1, a known substrate of LUBAC, in the TNF complex is linearly ubiquitinated in at increased levels.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claims.claim: HOIL-1L catalytic activity negatively regulates ubiquitination of substrates in cells.
claims.source: These data indicate that the HOIL-1L catalytic activity negatively regulates ubiquitination of the substrates in cells, which also supports our observations in vitro.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and comparison to literature.

results.result: The authors developed a co-expression strategy in insect cells to purify high-quality recombinant LUBAC, overcoming previous challenges with individual component purification in E. coli.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C31 demonstrate a clear methodological advance. The poor yields and contaminants from E. coli expression (C28) are explained by HOIP instability without partners (C29), and the insect cell co-expression strategy successfully produced pure LUBAC (C30, C31) as shown in Figures 1B-C.

results.result: Gel filtration analysis revealed that purified LUBAC exists in multiple oligomeric states with peaks containing all three components being stable and not prone to dissociation.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C35 are well-supported by gel filtration data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1. The elution profile shows distinct peaks (C32), with peaks I and II containing all components (C33) while peak III contains partial complexes (C34), and tandem gel filtration confirms stability (C35).

results.result: The authors generated the first 3D reconstruction of LUBAC using negative stain electron microscopy, revealing an elongated asymmetric crescent structure.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C36-C38, and C95 are strongly supported by electron microscopy data in Figure 2. The monodisperse particle distribution (C36), successful 3D reconstruction (C37), and elongated structure (C38, C95) are clearly demonstrated with appropriate validation through 2D class averages and projections.

results.result: Mass photometry measurements determined that LUBAC exists as monomers (231 kDa) and dimers (454 kDa) with a 1:1:1 stoichiometry between HOIP, HOIL-1L, and SHARPIN.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C40 are supported by mass photometry data in Figure 2D. The measured masses of 231 kDa and 454 kDa closely match the expected masses for monomeric (222 kDa) and dimeric (444 kDa) LUBAC with 1:1:1 stoichiometry, providing strong evidence for the complex composition.

results.result: Cross-linking mass spectrometry revealed extensive inter- and intra-protein interactions within LUBAC, including proximity between the catalytic RBR domains of HOIP and HOIL-1L.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C51 and C6 are well-supported by XL-MS data in Figure 3. The extensive cross-link network (C44), identification of flexible regions (C45-C46), and critical cross-links between HOIP and HOIL-1L RBR domains (C47-C48) provide strong structural evidence for spatial organization and suggest coordinated catalytic activity (C49, C51).

results.result: Based on cross-linking data and functional studies, the authors propose that LUBAC has a single catalytic center containing the RBR domains of both HOIP and HOIL-1L, operating through a coordinated ubiquitin relay mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C52, C100, C7, and C96 represent mechanistic proposals based on proximity data (C99) and logical inference (C98). While the cross-linking data support spatial proximity, the claims about a 'single catalytic center' and the specific relay mechanism are speculative interpretations that require additional structural and functional validation.

results.result: Co-purified LUBAC generates ubiquitin chains with additional signals absent from reactions with individually mixed components, indicating that proper complex assembly is required for full catalytic activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C55 are supported by data in Figure 4A-B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2. The ATP-dependent chain assembly (C53), unique signals from co-purified LUBAC (C54), and mass photometry showing that mixing components doesn't form the complex (C55) provide strong evidence that pre-assembly is necessary.

results.result: LUBAC assembles heterotypic ubiquitin chains containing predominantly linear linkages with non-lysine-linked branches, as demonstrated using various ubiquitin mutants including K0.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C57 and C61 are well-supported by data in Figure 4C-D. The observation that all KR mutants (C56) and even K0 ubiquitin (C57) can be used to generate heterotypic chains provides strong evidence that the branching involves non-lysine linkages (C61).

results.result: UbiCRest analysis using linkage-specific DUBs revealed that LUBAC-assembled chains contain linear linkages (OTULIN-sensitive) and non-linear di- and tri-ubiquitin species (Cezanne and vOTU-sensitive).
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C60 are supported by UbiCRest data in Figure 4E. The differential sensitivity to Cezanne/vOTU (C58-C59) versus OTULIN (C60) provides clear evidence for heterotypic chain composition, though the interpretation that Cezanne targets Lys11 linkages may be complicated by its esterase activity discovered later.

results.result: LUBAC generates heterotypic ubiquitin chains containing linear linkages with oxyester-linked branches, as demonstrated by hydroxylamine sensitivity and dependence on HOIL-1L catalytic activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C63, C4, and C5 are strongly supported by hydroxylamine treatment data (Figure 5A) and catalytic mutant studies (Figure 7). The disappearance of the upper band upon hydroxylamine treatment (C62) indicates oxyester bonds (C63), and this is the central finding of the manuscript (C4, C5).

results.result: When the N-terminus of ubiquitin is blocked (His-ubiquitin), LUBAC can still assemble hydroxylamine-sensitive oxyester-linked poly-ubiquitin chains, demonstrating that oxyester bond formation can occur independently of linear chain assembly.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C65 are supported by data in Figure 5B. The ability to form hydroxylamine-sensitive chains with His-ubiquitin, which cannot form linear chains, provides strong evidence that HOIL-1L can catalyze oxyester-linked ubiquitin polymerization independently.

results.result: Combined treatment with OTULIN and hydroxylamine completely degrades LUBAC-assembled poly-ubiquitin chains, demonstrating that LUBAC assembles exclusively linear and oxyester linkages between ubiquitin moieties.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C67 are supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A. The complete degradation of ubiquitin chains by sequential OTULIN and hydroxylamine treatment provides strong evidence that no other linkage types are present in significant amounts.

results.result: Mass spectrometry analysis identified Thr12 and Thr55 as sites of oxyester bond formation in ubiquitin, with these residues positioned at opposite sides of the ubiquitin molecule.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C69 and C103 are supported by MS/MS data in Figure 5C and structural analysis in Figure 5D. The detection of GG-conjugated dipeptides at Thr12 and Thr55 (C68, C103) and their spatial positioning (C69) are clearly demonstrated.

results.result: Mutation of Thr12 and/or Thr55 did not abolish heterotypic chain assembly, suggesting that linear chain branching is not strictly site-specific and that secondary sites exist.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C71 and C104 are supported by data in Figure 5E. The persistence of chain branching with T12V, T55V, and T12/55V mutants provides strong evidence for multiple potential branching sites, though this somewhat contradicts the MS identification of specific sites.

results.result: TNF stimulation of MEFs induces formation of ubiquitin chains containing both linear linkages and hydroxylamine-sensitive ester bonds, demonstrating that heterotypic chains are produced in cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C74 and C8 are supported by data in Figure 6A. The TNF-induced increase in linear chains (C72) that are sensitive to hydroxylamine (C73) provides strong evidence that heterotypic chains form in cells during physiological signaling (C74, C8).

results.result: Analysis of NEMO ubiquitination suggests that oxyester branch points are located distally from the substrate, and linear ubiquitin chains are not conjugated to NEMO via oxyester bonds.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C77, C108-C109 are supported by data in Figure 6B. The partial hydroxylamine sensitivity (C75) with most signal unperturbed (C76) indicates that substrate conjugation is primarily through isopeptide bonds (C77, C109) with branching occurring distally (C108).

results.result: LUBAC containing catalytically inactive HOIL-1L (C460A) generates only linear chains without the heterotypic branching pattern, demonstrating that HOIL-1L is responsible for ester-linked branch formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C81 and C5 are strongly supported by data in Figure 7A. The absence of the double band pattern with HOIL-1L C460A (C80) provides direct evidence that HOIL-1L catalytic activity is required for branch formation (C81, C5).

results.result: HOIP assembles longer linear ubiquitin chains more rapidly in the absence of HOIL-1L catalytic activity, while HOIP catalytic activity is absolutely required for any ubiquitin polymerization, suggesting that HOIL-1L activity disturbs but depends on HOIP activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C84 are supported by data in Figure 7A and consistent with prior literature. The enhanced linear chain assembly without HOIL-1L activity (C82), complete loss with HOIP C885A (C83), and the inference about their relationship (C84) are well-demonstrated.

results.result: OTULIN restriction analysis confirms that wild-type LUBAC produces non-linear di- and tri-ubiquitin chains, while HOIL-1L C460A-containing LUBAC generates exclusively linear chains.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C86 are supported by data in Figure 7B. The differential OTULIN sensitivity between wild-type and C460A LUBAC provides independent confirmation of the role of HOIL-1L in generating non-linear linkages.

results.result: In HOIL-1L C458A knock-in MEFs, TNF-induced linear ubiquitin chains are not sensitive to hydroxylamine treatment and show elevated basal levels, demonstrating that ester-linked branching in cells depends on HOIL-1L catalytic activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C91 and C9 are strongly supported by data in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 2D. The loss of hydroxylamine sensitivity (C90) with maintained LUBAC expression (C87) and TNF response (C88) provides compelling cellular validation that HOIL-1L catalyzes ester-linked branching in vivo.

results.result: The HOIL-1L NZF domain is involved in chain branching, as the T203A/R210A mutant that disrupts linear ubiquitin binding partially impairs branching activity while increasing overall chain assembly efficiency.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C94 are supported by data in Figure 7E. The partial impairment of branching (C92) with intermediate chain assembly efficiency (C93) suggests that the NZF domain facilitates but is not absolutely required for branching, supporting a model where HOIL-1L binds linear chains for branching (C94).

results.result: LUBAC assembles heterotypic ubiquitin chains through the concerted action of HOIP and HOIL-1L, where HOIP assembles linear chains that are subsequently branched by HOIL-1L in a process involving its NZF domain.
results.evaluation: Claims C10 and C94 represent the main conclusion of the manuscript, supported by the collective evidence from catalytic mutants, NZF mutants, and cellular studies. The sequential model is well-supported, though the precise molecular mechanism remains to be fully elucidated.

results.result: Linear ubiquitin chains appear to be heavily branched in cells based on near-complete hydroxylamine sensitivity, while in vitro only small populations are branched, suggesting that additional cellular factors may assist HOIL-1L.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C115 identify an important discrepancy between cellular (C112-C113) and in vitro (C114) data. While the observations are valid, the speculation about additional factors (C115) is not directly tested. Alternative explanations (reaction time, substrate availability, complex stability) are not excluded.

results.result: Cezanne, a known negative regulator of NF-κB, can cleave ester-linked branches in vitro, suggesting it may have esterase activity and target LUBAC-assembled chains during NF-κB regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C118 present an interesting observation (C116) and speculation (C118). While Cezanne's ability to cleave ester bonds is demonstrated, its characterization as a Lys11-specific DUB (earlier in the manuscript) creates ambiguity. The speculation about physiological esterase activity (C118) requires direct testing.

results.result: HOIL-1L catalytic activity negatively regulates TNF-induced signaling and linear ubiquitination of substrates, as demonstrated by increased linear ubiquitination in HOIL-1L catalytic mutant cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C122 and C27 are supported by data in Figure 7C and citations to recent literature. The increased basal linear ubiquitination in C458A MEFs (C120) and consistency with prior reports (C119, C121) support the conclusion that HOIL-1L activity negatively regulates linear ubiquitination (C122, C27).

results.result: HOIP exclusively targets Met1 for polymerization while HOIL-1L has flexibility in target site selection, with differences between isolated HOIL-1L and HOIL-1L in LUBAC suggesting that HOIP and SHARPIN may contribute to site selection.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C102 are well-established (C101 supported by citation), but C105-C107 involve speculation about how HOIP and SHARPIN influence HOIL-1L site selection. The differences in identified sites (C105) are noted but not mechanistically explained. Claims C106-C107 are speculative and lack direct experimental support.

results.result: Loss of HOIL-1L catalytic activity impairs but does not prevent substrate ubiquitination, suggesting that HOIL-1L is not responsible for priming substrates with mono-ubiquitin for HOIP extension.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C111 are supported by citation (C110) and inference from the NEMO data (C111). The observation that substrate ubiquitination persists without HOIL-1L activity, combined with the hydroxylamine insensitivity of substrate conjugation, supports the conclusion that HOIL-1L does not prime substrates.
